title: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?

posts.topic_title: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.author: Justin W
posts.post_subject: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.content_md:
Howdy all!

When I finally get a new lab built, I plan to start burning flexible film for the first time. Until now, I've been exposing on small glass plates. Plates were so easy! I frankly am finding the thought of dealing with flexible silver halide film rather daunting.

I'll be coming in from overhead with my reference beam - vertically polarized and illuminating the film sandwich at Brewster's - and would use a dry sandwich if I could. However, I read time and again things that have been written that say for all intents and purposes that I can expect at best mediocre holograms without index matching...

I believe I understand the reason for index matching - to make the passage from that first sheet of glass into the film as "seamless" as possible... The light won't feel inclined to reflect if it doesn't think it's seeing a surface, yah?

Lamp oil comes highly recommended but my lord that sounds like a messy hassle! I don't relish the thought of having to handle the film enough to wash off an oil before development - ug.

Glycerin, however, is clear, viscous and water soluble - yay!

BUT.... Is also classified as a sugar alcohol and a humectant. Will it swell my emulsion while all I'm asking it to do is match indices of refraction?

I'm shooting with green light and frankly don't want anything to do with a pre-swell. Aside from the potential for blue-shift, I also cringe at the thought of this swelling leading to movement of the film. What can I say... I'm a worrywart.

My question being: Will glycerin work OK for index matching of VRP-M film between glass sheets during exposure? I understand VRP-M to be your basic silver halide emulsion (60-80 microns thick) on triacetate substrate 180 microns thick.

All input welcome! (short of rocks chucked at my head)

Many thanks and respect.

posts.topic_title: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.author: Martin
posts.post_subject: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.content_md:
> **Justin W:** Lamp oil comes highly recommended but my lord that sounds like a messy hassle! I don't relish the thought of having to handle the film enough to wash off an oil before development - ug.

Instead of lamp oil (paraffin), you could try a couple of solvents also – see [http://www.holowiki.com/index.php/Index_Matching](http://www.holowiki.com/index.php/Index_Matching).

White spirit and alike may be much easier to remove from your emulsion: prior to development you'd simply apply a hair dryer to have the solvent evaporate.

> Glycerin, however, is clear, viscous and water soluble - yay!BUT.... Is also classified as a sugar alcohol and a humectant. Will it swell my emulsion while all I'm asking it to do is match indices of refraction?

Glycerol is likely to introduce a lot of instability to your emulsion. Depending on your lab's environment, it may attract considerable amounts of water (from air “humidity”). Moreover, small quantities of glycerol may get absorbed by the triacetate film base.

> I'm shooting with green light and frankly don't want anything to do with a pre-swell. Aside from the potential for blue-shift, I also cringe at the thought of this swelling leading to movement of the film. What can I say... I'm a worrywart.

It's true the TEA pretreatment can be messy.

Put aside the blue shift, TEA may have the benefit of doubling film speed.

> My question being: Will glycerin work OK for index matching of VRP-M film between glass sheets during exposure? I understand VRP-M to be your basic silver halide emulsion (60-80 microns thick) on triacetate substrate 180 microns thick.

Due to the instabilities glycerin is causing, I wouldn't use it.

Emulsion thickness is 6-8 microns.

And FILMOTEC film might be an alternative to VRP-M.

posts.content_md:
Kool.

Thank you everyone for your valued contributions and saintly patience in the face of my powerful ignorance.

Martin - That's extremely notable regarding the likelyhood of the substrate itself absorbing what I had erroneously hoped was a fairly inert goo. Sounds unstable! TEA? I never mentioned triethanolamine but thank you for bringing it up, for it leads me to Segue #1 (see below)

Ed and Danny - This open faced sandwich sounds delicious. Any suggestions on reasonably fast green-sensitive film that is flat enough for such an endeavour? I've only got 17.1mW to burn with and even numbers like 250µjoules for reflection (filmotec's fastest) sounds like a looooooong exposure compared to the 75µjoules required for VRP-M (film I've heard has a burning yearning desire to curl)...?

Colin - My brother, I swear I checked the wiki Your efforts have not been for nothing. I read that about white spirits and will tap dance sideways into Segue #2...

But first, presenting....in numerical order:

Segue #1 Pretreatments - I have heard that TEA pretreatment of film (for the purpose of a pre-swell) will increase sensitivity and allow for shorter exposures. Is this result unique to triethanolamine or will any pretreatment hypersensitize film for having washed out some of the bromine? Perhaps more to the point: Will a pre-wash in distilled water hypersensitize to the same degree as a pretreatment in TEA?

Segue #2 White spirits for index matching - In my limited experience with volatile solvents, I've noted them in general to be very thin, very runny liquids. Will paint thinner etc stay in place between film and glass for long enough to settle and expose a glass/film/glass sandwich held vertically? That's my fear. I feel I'm asking a lot of capillary action to hold such wily liquid against gravity for that long....

Again, thanks to all

posts.topic_title: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.author: Martin
posts.post_subject: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.content_md:
> **Justin W:** Segue #1 Pretreatments - I have heard that TEA pretreatment of film (for the purpose of a pre-swell) will increase sensitivity and allow for shorter exposures. Is this result unique to triethanolamine or will any pretreatment hypersensitize film for having washed out some of the bromine? Perhaps more to the point: Will a pre-wash in distilled water hypersensitize to the same degree as a pretreatment in TEA?

No, TEA does provide more efficient hypersensitization than a water wash.

There are other means of hypersensitizing agents though – I think we've covered several of them here on the forum. TEA may be the one to have the least side effects (with respect to toxicity, fogging, grain growth etc.). And no, TEA won't wash out the silver bromide.

> **Justin W:** Segue #2 White spirits for index matching - In my limited experience with volatile solvents, I've noted them in general to be very thin, very runny liquids. Will paint thinner etc stay in place between film and glass for long enough to settle and expose a glass/film/glass sandwich held vertically? That's my fear. I feel I'm asking a lot of capillary action to hold such wily liquid against gravity for that long....

That's been my experience the last time I did that with PFG-01 or PFG-03 film. But that's been a while ago. I heard Slavich had improved their TAC substrate film in the meantime. I believe their emulsion now is coated on a 250um TAC film (compared to 180um or something like that previously).

With the Slavich films I managed to get high stability by index matching a plexi sheet on top of the film (which in turn had been index matched on a glass plate). That allowed exposure times up to 15 minutes.

Agfa used to produce films that could easily be index matched with white spirit etc. on a glass plate – no sandwiching (additional glass plate) was required.

Regarding Filmotec, I gathered they acquired one of the Agfa devices to make triacetate film on their own. So this might be good news with regards to the film curling issue.

I was using small pieces of film to test laser diodes and had to run through 25 or so tests a night. I tried every clear liquid I could get at the local hardware store. The highest grade of lamp oil was the easiest for me to use but even MEK did not run out of a vertical sandwich. I rinsed the lamp oil in a bath of distilled water and dropped straight into the developer. I am certian there was lots of cross contamination going on but it seemed to work fine. 

In the new lab there will be running water!

Wow!

Thank you everybody for kickin' me some useful information.

Sounds like I have once again found myself in the realm of "whatever works"...

Perhaps theres been an element of synchronicity to this post - While there's no real link between TEA and the act of index matching flexible film, maybe just maybe there's some merit in experimenting with:

1. Pressing VRP-M film sheets between glass for a few days in a darkened fridge to try to flatten them

2. Soaking sheet of film in TEA/water pretreatment bath

3. Removing film and squeegying to glass

4. Mounting glass, settling, exposing (at dramatically reduced exposure time)

5. Washing TEA from film

6. Developing/bleaching

7. Post-swelling

8. Drying

9. Bragging and carrying on in general

Worth experimentation 

-or-

A very time consuming yet effective way of wasting some expensive film

???

posts.post_subject: Stupid idea?: Index matching with glycerin?
posts.content_md:
Hello Everyone,

Heres another method that I've used many times. Its never been a problem.

Take your film and laminate it down to glass, emulsion out, using a water clear adhesive that is non-birefringent. I used Permatrans from MacTac. I'm sure there are others. They might call their products something else by now.

After you lam the film to the glass let it “set” for a day or more. You will notice it gets nice and flat. After that....you have a glass plate! None of our chemistry will mess with the adhesive, it will never turn yellow or anything like that. I have masters that are 20 years old produced this way. Not one has failed over the years.

This type of adhesive is a plastic carrier with adhesive on both sides. Also on both sides is a clear poly release liner. What I used to do was peel one side, lam the film down and trim the adhesive so it was slightly larger than the film. I would then peel the other side and laminate it to glass. Then I cut off the excess laminate with a razor and peel it off the glass. 

I used to do 4x5's with a cheap hand roller from the art supply store, worked like a charm if you keep things clean. Back then I did not have any clean hood equipment. Just windex and some paper towels. 

I also bonded the film to glass that was 1/4 inch thick. It was very nice working with plates that thick.

Good luck

 Jeffrey Weil

 NorthBeach Holography Inc.

P.S. Anybody that sends me a self addressed, stamped envelope will get a free sample of this adhesive to give it a try!
